paragraphs.text: This [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) brick was pressed in Yunnan in 1990 and has been kept in Guangzhou’s tea trade in the decades since. It dates from the early years of the style: Yunnan’s state factories only brought [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) into production in 1973, after a joint team studied faster piling in Guangdong.
Thirty-six years on, it belongs to [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged), where the place a tea was kept shapes it as much as the years it has spent there.

brewing.text: Work a piece loose from the edge of the brick with a pick instead of breaking it off. Use boiling water, about 7 grams to 100 ml, one quick rinse, then short steeps that grow longer as the leaf opens. Ripe tea forgives a heavy hand, and an old brick like this gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
